title: Earth Has a Temporary Second Moon: Asteroid 2026 QQ8 Will Orbit Us Until Early December

content:
Earth has a second moon — for now. A small asteroid about 2 meters wide, designated 2026 QQ8, has been captured by Earth’s gravity and is orbiting our planet as a temporary “mini-moon,” scientists confirmed this week. It is expected to drift away in early December.

The object was discovered in August by Krisztián Sárneczky, research coordinator at Konkoly Observatory in Hungary. On Oct. 29, the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center announced that the object was trapped in Earth’s gravity and gave it the designation 2026 QQ8.

Follow-up observations with the Lowell Discovery Telescope in Arizona and the 2.2-meter telescope at Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii confirmed that 2026 QQ8 is a naturally formed celestial body, not a piece of space debris. At about 2 meters across, it is far too small and faint to see with the naked eye, and it is difficult even for telescopes to tell apart from artificial satellites and their debris.

Not the first mini-moon

2026 QQ8 belongs to a class of near-Earth objects that get temporarily captured by Earth. Previous known mini-moons include 2006 RH120, which circled Earth for about a year, and 2020 CD3, which stayed for about three years. Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center, said that on average, scientists estimate there is roughly one mini-moon around Earth at any given time — most are very small and move quickly, making them extremely hard to detect.

Research is still underway to pin down where 2026 QQ8 came from. Most near-Earth objects are thought to originate in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, where gravitational interactions over millions of years can send some bodies toward the inner solar system.

There is no chance of a collision, according to current analyses. Even if the tiny rock entered Earth’s atmosphere, it would break apart without causing significant damage — at most, Payne said, observers would see a bright meteor streak across the sky and hear a small explosion-like sound.

Sources: DongA Science, Nov. 22, 2026 (reporting on CNN and the International Astronomical Union Minor Planet Center); NASA/JPL-Caltech.
